summary: Catalogs known TCP implementation problems with Path MTU Discovery, including the long-standing black hole problem and confusion between the maximum segment size and the path's packet size limits. It is informational and suggests fixes.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a big package cannot fit through a narrow tunnel and silently disappears. This lists the ways computers get stuck there and how to avoid it.

subtitle: A catalog of three TCP bugs that make Path MTU Discovery hang connections, slow ACKs or shrink segments.

tldr.problem: Path MTU Discovery depends on routers sending ICMP messages, and some TCP implementations handle its side effects badly, so connections can hang or perform poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes three problems in a fixed template (classification, description, traces, how to detect, how to fix): black hole detection, stretch ACKs due to PMTUD, and determining the MSS from the PMTU.
tldr.outcome: It is informational. It recommends that TCP notice repeated timeouts and send smaller packets, ACK based on received segment size, and set the advertised MSS from interface MTUs.

facts.label: Typical black hole symptom
facts.value: Connection ends after 15 minutes with zero bytes transferred

today: RFC 2923 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows it neither obsoleted nor updated. It documents problems and advice rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Template
sections.content:
This memo catalogs known TCP implementation problems with Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD, RFC 1191). The goal is to improve the existing Internet by raising the quality of TCP/IP implementations. It covers TCP only, and does not treat problems of other upper-layer protocols or IPv6-specific issues (see RFC 1981).

Each problem is described with the same fields: name, classification (congestion control, performance, reliability or non-interoperation), description, significance, implications, relevant RFCs, trace files showing the problem and correct behavior, references, how to detect and how to fix. The structure comes from RFC 2525.
sections.eli5: The memo fills in the same checklist for each problem, like a doctor's chart: what it is, who it hurts, how to spot it and how to cure it.

sections.title: Black Hole Detection
sections.content:
A host does PMTUD by sending the largest packet it can with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set. A router that cannot forward it must send back an ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed message. Many routers fail to, because of kernel bugs or configuration problems, and firewalls are often misconfigured to suppress all ICMP. The sender then keeps sending large packets that vanish into a PMTUD black hole.

This is classed as non-interoperation, a connectivity failure. It is hard to debug because pings and some interactive TCP connections work, while bulk transfers fail on the first large packet and the connection eventually times out. The memo notes it often shows as a connection that transfers nothing and ends after 15 minutes, and that ftp works for control traffic and then fails on bulk transfers.

The fix: after several timeouts TCP should try smaller packets, perhaps turning DF off for each packet. If that works, it should leave PMTUD off for the connection for a reasonable period and then probe again. IPv6 has no DF bit, but its minimum MTU is 1280 octets (against 68 octets for IPv4), so falling back is easier. Ideally the ICMP black holes themselves get fixed, and hosts that detect black holes should probably log them, since detection can take several seconds each time and hide a performance loss.
sections.eli5: A truck too wide for a tunnel is supposed to get a warning sign. If the sign is missing, the truck just keeps trying. The fix is for the driver to switch to smaller trucks after a few failures.

sections.title: Stretch ACKs Caused by PMTUD
sections.content:
A naive TCP receiver tries to acknowledge every second full-sized segment. If it decides what is full-sized from the advertised MSS, this breaks down when PMTUD makes the real path limit a small fraction of that MSS: ACKs are then generated only very rarely. These are called stretch ACKs.

The memo classes this as congestion control and performance. Stretch ACKs encourage bursty connections because ACKs arrive infrequently, and they can impede congestion window growth (details in RFC 2525). The traces show the ACK interval is almost exactly two times the advertised MSS, rather than two times the segment size actually sent.

Two fixes are offered. The simple one is to ACK every other packet regardless of size, though that creates many ACKs when applications send lots of tiny packets, as the X Window System does. The slightly more complex one monitors incoming segment sizes to infer the sender's segment size, which needs a little more receiver state but makes receiver silly window syndrome avoidance more accurate.
sections.eli5: If you only clap after every two songs but the songs shrink to tiny snippets, you almost never clap. The fix is to count the actual snippets you hear.

sections.title: Determining the MSS from the PMTU
sections.content:
The MSS a host advertises at connection start should be based on the MTUs of its own interfaces. Some systems instead use a value learned earlier by PMTUD, so the advertised MSS ends up smaller than the largest MTU the system can receive.

This is classed as a performance problem. The advertised MSS tells the remote side the largest segment it can receive (RFC 879), so a too-small value forces smaller segments only because of an earlier path finding. Routes are often asymmetric, so the return PMTU may differ, and an artificially low limit makes it impossible to probe later for a larger PMTU. The memo notes this practice does not violate any specification in the RFCs it cites.

In the memo's two-connection trace, the second connection from host A advertises an MSS of 984 after the first learned an MTU of 1024 at a bottleneck router. In the correct trace both connections use the same MSS. To detect it, compare two back-to-back connections. The fix is to set the MSS from interface MTUs as in RFC 1122 and RFC 1191.
sections.eli5: If one road was narrow yesterday, you should not tell everyone to send only tiny parcels forever. Say what your own door allows and let the road be tested again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The one security concern raised is that ICMP black holes are often caused by over-zealous security administrators who block all ICMP messages. The memo says designers and deployers of security systems must understand the impact of strict filtering on upper-layer protocols, and that it would be far nicer to fix all black holes than to fix all TCP implementations.
sections.eli5: If a guard blocks every warning sign, trucks get stuck. Guards need to know which signs must be let through.

viz.caption: THE THREE PROBLEMS AT A GLANCE

cells: After several timeouts, try smaller packets and probe again later
ACK every other packet, or track incoming segment sizes
Set the MSS from interface MTUs
